Reddit pivots to a login-only experience

2026-11-11

Reddit announced it will soon require users to log in to see much of the helpful human-generated content on its site. Why? Because traffic, and thus advertising, has taken a hit since AI started summarizing its data.

It's the latest development to threaten the old model of the open internet, says Sarah Gilbert, who researches online communities at the Citizens and Technology Lab at Cornell and is also active in r/askhistorians. She says the new login requirement puts up a wall between humans on the internet and is likely to discourage future contributions to the site.

‘Hell sucks.’ A veteran reflects on life and death at the DMZ, 1967

2026-11-11

Author’s note: This year is the 60th anniversary of my deployment to South Vietnam, a milestone I commemorate by rerunning this piece, which I posted a couple of years ago – John Tsitrian

It’s Veterans Day and I’m revisiting the Nam.

In the above pic, I had just come back to the relatively secure airstrip at Dong Ha, slightly south of the Demilitarized Zone, after spending a few weeks at some — pick an adjective, they all fit — desolate, remote, bleak, lonely, dark, depressing, forlorn, gloomy, wretched and neglected outpost along the nearby Cua Viet river, where rocket and artillery attacks were part of the daily routine and potshots into our perimeter were an occasional part of the nightly routine.

It sucked, and it wasn’t just about me. Describing life for all the Marines along the DMZ, Dispatches author Michael Herr titled his piece about us “Hell Sucks.”

That pretty well summed it up.

It was at the DMZ that I had my first encounter with incomprehensibility and surrealism, where waste of materials and humans was supposed to be an acceptable consequence of an American crusade to fight off, in then President Lyndon Johnson’s words, “the deepening shadow of Communist China,” which was a principal source of supplies and weapons to our enemy, North Vietnam. Together, the Chinese and the North Vietnamese were characterized by American cold warriors as “the yellow peril.”

Johnson sold the war to the American public with that kind of rhetoric, but it turned out to be baloney.

How’s that? Well, in 1972 with the war still raging, LBJ’s successor Richard Nixon set out to make friends with China, even though Chinese weaponry was still targeting and killing American troops. Despite that, Nixon was proudly and optimistically visiting Beijing. He was busy opening up trade and diplomatic channels with the country that LBJ just a few years earlier described as a fearsome spectre and “deepening shadow.”

Confused? I was.

Was China LBJ’s threat to the free world, or was it Nixon’s friend and potential diplomatic and trading partner? The war was so messed up that the two presidents of the era couldn’t get their stories straight.

To me, it’s little wonder that so many Vietnam vets have had post-war mental health issues. The confused situation of our war was indeed surreal, if not altogether schizophrenic. A 2022 Veterans Administration study on the subject concluded that “veterans who served in Vietnam, Cambodia, or Laos during the Vietnam War have a higher prevalence of mental health issues, particularly PTSD, compared with both other Vietnam-era Veterans and non-Veterans.”

The whole mangled mess of it was an exercise in muddled objectives and wasted resources, so much so that when people died we didn’t say that they were killed. We said that they “got wasted.”

Now, nearly sixty years later, I’m a generally appreciated veteran. I couldn’t be more pleased. I like my status, but must note that thanks to that war, I also couldn’t be more skeptical about the utterances of our political leadership. That coarsened attitude has pushed me to speak out via my earlier stints as a feature writer and newspaper columnist and now as the publisher and editor of this blog.

With my fellow vets on this Veterans Day, I thank you for your attention and appreciation – as well as your support and patience when it comes to encountering veterans who were permanently scarred by experiences like mine.

I also hope that as you acknowledge and honor our veterans, you do so with a commitment to exercise some critical thought when listening to the rhetoric of our political class. That would be a nice outcome when you think of what veterans sacrificed in pursuit of their service to our country.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

2026-11-10, updated: 2026-11-11

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

via Electrek Feed

Last week's midterm elections were a requiem for MAGA

2026-11-10, updated: 2026-11-11

I was road-tripping through Minnesota last weekend and couldn’t resist taking the pic above from my car. Sorry about the resolution, but the posting of a worn out Trump sign on a dilapidated building was too rich with symbolism to bypass.

After several years of its mobilization and coalescence, after institutionalization by the Trump administration, and after one policy failure followed by another and then another, the MAGA  movement is exhausted … and expunged.

Trump loyalists trying to tout tariffs and the righteousness of our war with Iran just got their political rear ends handed to them, some in states like Kansas, Mississippi and Texas where Republicans just don’t lose.

I’m as prone to gloat as the next guy and gladly broadcast my giddiness over the election results last Tuesday. It’s not so much that I’m pro-Democrat as it is that I’m anti-Trump.

From my perspective as a pre-Trump Republican, I’m hoping that my former party can see the light and understand the damage —no, carnage — that Trump has inflicted on the GOP.

The party has to cleanse itself of Trump’s ideological and political detritus. Examples?

  • On trade policy the GOP has to re-engage the principles of free trade that have been a cornerstone of conservatism since the 1950s and forward to the Reagan-Bush years

  • On immigration, Republicans have to go back to the days when they championed immigration.They understood that pro-immigration policies, including finding pathways to legalization for undocumented residents, were among the reasons that our economy prospered.

  • On alliances, Republicans have to go back to a time when they championed NATO, which Trump has said is “obsolete.” A unified front like NATO ensures that its members face threats side-by-side rather than in isolation.

  • Republicans need to redevelop a friendlier approach to our immediate neighbors Mexico and Canada. Why Trump feels he needs to pick a fight with Canada is beyond understanding.

  • Embracing science again would be a nice reversion back to the days when Republicans “had a great deal of confidence” in the scientific community. Dragging their feet on climate change and putting the scientifically-challenged Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., in charge of Health and Human Services are, on the face of it, evidence that Trump’s party doesn’t give a damn about science.,

Trump and MAGA are worn out and used up. They’re helplessly ineffective and increasingly irrelevant. The problems they promised to solve are as burdensome as ever. It's time for some collective introspection by the GOP. It’s time to render Donald Trump politically useless and leave him to his self-glorifying dreams of building pretentious monuments and promoting his own silly brand.

There’s work to be done, Republicans. Time to get started

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Sacramento Bee

October was warmest on record. Will Dems address climate change?

2026-11-09, updated: 2026-11-11

This year’s October was the warmest on record. Maybe more sobering is the news that it was the third consecutive month to exceed the warming threshold set by the 2016 Paris Climate Agreement, which was ratified by 194 countries, including the United States.

The U.S. pulled out of the agreement, first in 2017, then, after Biden rejoined the accord during his presidency, again in January 2025 because President Trump, after a decision that was widely supported by conservatives, said its allotment of timelines for compliance gave an economic advantage to China and other nations at the expense of the United States.

Others disagreed, but the decision stuck.

So where is the United States now on climate change? Not a very good place.

The University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute concludes that “climate change is no longer a problem for the distant future. The effects of climate change are being seen and felt today.” You can scan the report for a detailed summation of the economic effects of climate change. A general conclusion is that warming temperatures will cost the U.S. anywhere from one to four percent of GDP by the end of the century.

Of more specific relevance to a farm state like South Dakota, Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability says that “rising global temperatures will dampen the world’s capacity to produce food from most staple crops, even after accounting for economic development and adaptation by farmers.”

Looking at this year’s situation, South Dakota’s farmers have been hit hard by drought, with producers in Brookings, Deuel, Hyde, and Stanley counties getting financial assistance from USDA because of severe or extended drought designations. The USDA statement reads “this disaster declaration highlights the continuing impact that drought can have on agricultural communities.”

Note the words “continuing impact.”

Has the Trump administration done much about alleviating climate change?  No. In fact, his “drill, baby, drill” mantra is a direct assault on the whole notion that climate change is real and has to be addressed.

My hope is that the new congress, heavily weighted toward Democrats, will weigh in on climate change and bring some reality and substance into the U.S. approach toward it.

And now that Trump has been so severely weakened, politically, by last week’s Democratic tsunami, let’s hope that our all-GOP representation can understand South Dakota’s stake in the future of climate change – and maybe stand up for their constituents who are dealing with it every day.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Did voters disregard politics and feel they just couldn’t stand Trump ?

2026-11-07, updated: 2026-11-11

Hee’s a quick take on the election.

It’s been interesting and sometimes comical watching people explaining the election results with excuses, analyses, rationalizations, anger, finger pointing, and hindsight.

Inflation, war with Iran, corruption, and ICE tactics have been cited as reasons why the Donald Trump presidency and the MAGA ideas were so soundly rejected.

Those things, large and small, were all part of it -  but perhaps there was also something else at play.

For those on the fence over the issues and the state of the nation, maybe one conspicuous thing could have been what pushed them over the edge:

Trump is just plain unlikable.

He is seen as cruel, vindictive, corrupt, thin skinned, and egotistical beyond the scope of the word. And he lies as easily as he breathes.

Did some voters disregard politics and finally feel they just couldn’t stand him anymore?

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

Teaching financial advisors the depth behind tools and recipes

2026-11-06, updated: 2026-11-11

When you cook, do you follow a recipe precisely or adapt it as you go? My wife uses the second approach. She will make something extraordinary, and when I ask if she wrote down what she did, she has no idea. She tasted, adjusted, and added a little of this or that. I am the opposite. Give me a recipe, and I’m fine; just don’t ask me to be creative.

That’s probably why, in my long-ago first sales job in real estate, I initially relied on the decision tree the manager gave me. “If the client says this, go here. If they object, go there.” I tried to memorize every branch. If a customer said something that wasn’t on any of them, I had nothing.

You have probably sat across from someone like that, maybe an insurance agent reading from a script or a financial advisor going through a standard questionnaire without looking up. You can feel the difference when someone is rigidly following a recipe rather than listening to you and responding to your needs and concerns.

The difference matters when someone is handling your financial life. Most advisor training works tool-first. You learn the exercise, practice it, and repeat it until you know the recipe and master the skill.

Breanna Blaney, founder of the Anya Institute and creator of the Integrative Wealth Advisor certification, uses a different approach to train financial advisors. Before her students learn any client-facing tools, they spend months doing their own inner work, examining their own relationship with money and their own blind spots. Only then do they learn the techniques. “I teach people how to cook,” she says, “not what the recipe is.”

When I introduce the emotional side of money to my financial planning students at Golden Gate University, the most common reaction is shock that it was never part of their formal education. “This is hard,” they say when I ask them to sit quietly with their own thoughts for a few minutes. If it is that hard for them, imagine how difficult it is for a planner without that practice to guide clients through their money issues.

Jacob Moreno, the founder of psychodrama, used the phrase “getting on the balcony” to describe rising above the action to observe what is actually happening rather than reacting. A financial advisor on the balcony asks better questions, notices what you are not saying, and does not flinch when the conversation moves past the numbers. Blaney’s description for this is, “I’m looking at you. I’m seeing you first.”

In practice, that means the advisor does not default to running you through the same sequence of questions, exercises, or rote processes they use with every client. They will not rush past the emotion to get to the spreadsheet. If you need to talk about why you cannot bring yourself to sell your late parents’ house before you can discuss the tax implications, an advisor who has done their own work will follow you there.

If you are looking for a financial advisor, here are some clues that someone knows how to cook rather than just how to follow a recipe:

  1. They ask about your life before they ask about your portfolio.

  2. They listen and clarify before they offer advice.

  3. They can sit with a difficult subject without changing it.

  4. They have examined their own relationship with money before trying to guide yours.

For a financial advisor, having a recipe book of skills and processes is essential. Just as important is knowing when and how to tweak those recipes to give clients the service and support they need.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

via Market Place Tech Report

Farmers need help. Let’s see if a Dem-led congress can provide it

2026-11-05, updated: 2026-11-11

Though grain and soybean prices have come up a bit in recent months, the American Farm Bureau thinks that farmers will continue to see tough times. Prices for their crops just aren’t  keeping up with input costs, principally fertilizer and diesel fuel.

So far, the Trump administration’s policies haven’t been able to make much of a difference by way of financial relief, so the White House turned to making direct cash payments to farmers in order for many of them to stay afloat.

Much as I support federal financial aid in order to keep producers functioning – food security is priority number one – an efficiently structured relationship between farmers and policy-makers in Washington is what the ag industry needs.

The Trump administration has been helpless when it comes to framing policy that works for farmers, which makes cash bailouts a necessity and only extends official ineptitude.

Last night’s overwhelming rejection of Trump and his policies was driven in large part by rural states that turned on the president’s party. Though South Dakota didn’t participate in the political overhaul, farmers in our state will be impacted by the changes in ag policies that should materialize in D.C. next year.

The first order of business should be passing a Farm Bill. Agriculture is a high risk business, subjected to sometimes wild price fluctuations and the vagaries of weather. Farm bills provide safety nets that farmers and their lenders can depend on.

Farmers also need an administration that knows something about how trade policy can affect rural livelihoods. Trump’s wild and irrational trade wars have permanently altered the soybean market, and not for the better as far as American producers are concerned.

Now that Democrats from rural areas are part of the political landscape in D.C. we should expect better when it comes to dealing with the headstrong Trump, who up to now had a Republican congress green-lighting policies that drove crop prices down and pushed input prices up.

Will the Democrats perform? I think they will, especially as much of their newfound political strength comes from the rural districts that terminated their Republican reps yesterday.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Song sung blue? No. Last night was the Hallelujah Chorus sung blue

2026-11-04, updated: 2026-11-11

Last night’s rebuke of Donald Trump should be a long-needed slap in the GOP’s collective face. His party has needed to come out of its Trump-induced stupor for a long time.

Trump caused this because he has taken the Republican Party on a path that has veered away from long-standing conservative principles, creating problems that led to a sweeping rejection of him and his loyalists.

If Trump had been true to Republican principles, this wouldn’t have happened.

  • If Trump had followed traditional GOP practice and ideology, his tariff binge would not have occurred. Republicans have historically been champions of free trade. During the Reagan and Bush era, free trade initiatives, particularly the development of the World Trade Organization, were a top priority. Back in 2017, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds was writing about the benefits of trade agreements and their importance to South Dakota. Trump’s tariff agenda has been bad for South Dakota and the country in  general, particularly on the inflation front.

  • Trump’s rhetoric on immigration completely reversed the attitude that was prevalent during the Reagan-Bush era. Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric and policies have had a negative effect on the economy.

  • Trump’s energy policies, which lead to greater dependence on fossil fuels, have been a disaster. “Drill, baby, drill” is about the dumbest approach to energy management I can think of, and I think about it every time I have to shell out serious bucks for a tankful of gasoline.  George W. Bush was a strong supporter of renewable energy.  Why Trump won’t follow suit is a mystery.

The common denominator for the way Trump has turned away from policies common to his recent Republican predecessors in the White House is inflation – and clearly, inflation is one of the main causes of the discontent that led to last night’s debacle. Trump has created an identity crisis for his party, and the public has just shown that it has had enough of it.

Hallelujah.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

How Dick Nixon tried to kill South Dakota Senator Karl Mundt

2026-11-03, updated: 2026-11-11

Author’s note: The difference between a memoir and an autobiography is that a memoir tells the story as best the author can remember it.  An autobiography has to be fact-checked.  This falls into the category of mini-memoir.

As a young speech and social studies instructor at Eastern State Normal School in the 1930s in Madison, South Dakota, once upon a time a teacher college that is now known as Dakota State University, Karl Mundt developed a name for two reasons. He founded the National Forensics League, a speech and debate organization for high school students nationwide. He traveled around eastern South Dakota demonstrating his skill as a public speaker.  Soon the idea arose that it might be good if someday he might run for Congress. Since the Board of Regents could not abide political campaigning by its employees, Mundt was summoned to the Dean’s office.

You are an outstanding speech instructor, the Dean supposedly told him, and I do not want to lose you, but as a possible political candidate you cannot have a contract to teach here. “I do not need a contract,” Mundt replied. “I shall be happy to continue teaching, but if after two weeks there is no pay envelope in my mailbox, my enthusiasm for teaching will wane considerably.”

In 1938 he won a seat in Congress, then later the Senate. He was on the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he taught young California Congressman Richard Nixon how to hunt Commies. In 1954 Mundt chaired the Army-McCarthy hearings.  He rose to become second-ranking Republican on the Appropriations Committee and delivered a fair amount of pork to South Dakota.

In 1969 he suffered a major stroke. His wife Mary, whom he met and married at University, believed he would recover and rebuffed efforts to have Karl step aside. As 1970 dawned it became clear that a Democrat might defeat Governor Frank Farrar and win the Governorship, and with it the ability to appoint a replacement to Mundt if he should die in office. Republican leaders wanted him to resign so Republican Farrar could appoint a replacement before the Democrats took the Governor’s Mansion.

First a hometown delegation of Republicans appeared at the door to Mundt’s home on Capitol Hill. Mary fussed in the kitchen and made coffee for them. We must protect this seat for the GOP, they argued.  Karl deserves to enjoy well-earned retirement. Mary scolded them for being disloyal.

Next a delegation of statewide Republican leaders knocked on the door.  A gracious welcome, but same thing. Shame on you, she said.

South Dakota’s Republican Governor Frank Farrar also tried, but that had no chance. Farrar had been floating the idea of running against Karl in the 1972 Republican primary. Mary adamantly opposed Karl’s resigning if it meant Farrar might appoint himself to the Senate seat.

Not long after that a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt residence.  Out came the President of the United States, Richard M. Nixon. He walked to the door and knocked. Mary welcomed him in. “Oh, Mr. President, Karl will be so happy to see you.” Mundt was sitting on a couch and may have been cognizant but, because of his stroke, was unable to string words together — a horrible loss for such a powerful orator.

While Mary was in the kitchen fussing to make coffee, the Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces turned to the young Naval orderly who was helping care for the Senator. Nixon pointed to cigar boxes on the top shelf of a bookcase. “What are those?” he asked.

“We have to constantly hide cigars from the Senator,” was the reply. “The doctor says if he smokes another he will have a big stroke and die."

Thereafter, once a week a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt home and a representative of the White House personally handed the Senator a box of cigars from President Nixon.

Jody Severson is a retired political and marketing consultant whose first campaign was "Clean for Gene" McCarthy in 1968.  He was a consultant in scores of campaigns at the statewide, local, and national levels from the north woods of Minnesota to the bayous of Louisiana. A native of Madison, SD, he has lived in Rapid City since the 1980s.

Photo: Then U.S. Representative Karl Mundt, 1940, public domain, wikimedia commons

My wish list if there is a blue wave in tomorrow’s election

2026-11-02, updated: 2026-11-11

If the Democrats take Congress tomorrow, fixing Trump’s mess should be the first item on the legislative agenda.

From an ag-oriented South Dakotan’s perspective, I want to see Congress undo the president’s tariffs.  It has the power to do so. They’ve been such a drag on our country’s farm economy that getting rid of them will loosen up long-standing supply chain disruptions and get some liquidity back into the world’s distribution networks.

Congress should use all the tools at its disposal to get Trump to end his useless war in Iran. Its inflationary impact and waste of lives and money need to cease.

Problems of affordability have to be addressed, and they will be if tariffs are rescinded and the Iran war comes to a close. More broadly, Congress can address the affordability crisis through legislative actions aimed at housing supply, tax policy, and health care costs.

Given the way climate change is accelerating, we need more in in the way of green energy incentives and fossil fuel regulation.

Immigration policy should be focused on getting undocumented but otherwise law-abiding immigrants on the pathways to legalization. This was Ronald Reagan’s approach, and it worked. Trump’s policy of rounding them up and deporting them wholesale amounts to a deplorable lack of humanity. If you have a Judeo-Christian bent, read Leviticus 19:33-34. If you’re focused on the practical, economic consequences of Trump’s heavy-handed policy, consider that it’s causing a labor shortage in this country.

The list is long and complex, but a resounding political mandate tomorrow will at least make it approachable.

Let’s get out there and vote.

via Sacramento Bee

We have a winner in the Iran war, and the winner is …

2026-10-31, updated: 2026-11-11

… the oil industry and its shareholders. Glancing across yesterday’s earning reports on the financial sites, the first headline I encountered in The Wall Street Journal announced “American Oil Giants See Profits Soar as Wars Crimp Energy Supplies.” The sub-head? “ExxonMobil and Chevron post blockbuster earnings for third quarter as world turns to U.S. refineries for fuel.”

ExxonMobil’s profits doubled compared to the same period last year. Chevron’s were up 185%. Meantime, we consumers are gagging at our local gas pumps, paying an average of $4.12/gallon, about a buck over what we were paying a year ago.

This is what Donald Trump has wrought.

Though he has since claimed that he was misinterpreted, Trump at the onset of the war said that it would be over in a matter of weeks. Since then the timeline has shifted. The last I heard, he said the war will end “soon,” a comfortably meaningless word when it comes to specificty. That and his claims of being misunderstood only amplify his incoherence on the subject.

That Trump [recently said](https://“We’re in the golden age of America. So our nation is doing better now than ever before,”) “we’re in the golden age of America … our nation is doing better now than ever before” only amplifies his detachment from reality.

Meanwhile, as the back and forth on what-Trump-said vs. what-Trump-meant goes on, the practical effect of Trump’s invasion of Iran has been to make oil producers much, much richer and helpless oil consumers all the poorer.

As to the president trying to do something about high fuel costs, Trump has come up way short. His feeble efforts to ease diesel fuel prices by engineering a deal that would let Russia increase diesel fuel exports were a fantasy ( Foreign Policy calls the deal a “hail Mary”) from the get-go. Not only have diesel prices not gone down, they’ve actually risen by 7 cents/gallon since the deal was announced.

On the gasoline front, Trump’s only utterances about potentially lower prices are that gas will get cheaper once the Iran war ends. That stands to reason, but the price-dropping process will be slow-going once the Strait of Hormuz opens."If and when that happens, it will be a very long, multi-month to multi-year process for things to fully normalize,"  says a GasBuddy petroleum expert quoted on CBS.

The economically painful results of Trump’s hapless venture into the Persian Gulf will linger for a long time. The Center for Strategic and International Studies sees localized conflicts, many of them stirred up during Trump’s incursion into the area, as a “postwar threat to Gulf energy infrastructure.”

Unclear as Trump’s objectives in this war have been, his options seem even more muddled, which is a natural follow-up to the discordant statements and erratic strategies that got us into this mess in the first place.

via NPR Economic

Why artificial intelligence can’t replace your financial planner

2026-10-30, updated: 2026-11-11

What is a financial planner worth when anyone can get a plan from ChatGPT? A student asked this question during a recent video call with the Wealth Management Society at Brigham Young University–Idaho. Here is my answer.

AI can already read financial documents, run a tax analysis, and estimate how long retirement savings may last. It is getting good at supplying answers that can help build a sound technical plan. I expect more people to arrive at a planner’s office having done much of that work themselves, so the conversation can start at a higher level.

Yet the logical answers AI gives are of limited value in making money decisions, which are seldom made on logic alone. Stanford marketing professor Baba Shiv has suggested that 90 to 95 percent of our decisions are shaped by emotion without our being aware of it. If money decisions were logical, nobody would overspend, everyone would live within a budget, and every worker would be saving for retirement.

People who are stuck on a money decision usually do not need another answer. They need someone to listen long enough for them to reach their own answer. In my early years as a financial planner, I was the advice and answer man. I couldn’t see why anyone would turn down my logical and correct advice. I learned, painfully, to shut up until it was time to give advice, and then to ask permission first.

For example, a client in my financial therapy practice came in for a recent session stuck on a decision between three options I will call A, B, and C. Almost immediately, I thought B was the answer. Instead of saying so, I got curious and asked questions, and we spent the whole hour looking at what each option meant to her. At the end she said, “I think the answer is B for me.”

I could have given her that answer right away, which is what a chatbot might have done. In my experience, though, people are far more likely to act on an answer they reach themselves than on one someone hands them.

My intent is not to discourage anyone from using AI with their money. I use it to manage my calendar and email and to analyze my financial documents, and I’m often amazed at what it finds.

Here are my suggestions for using AI with your finances:

  • If you are researching a financial decision, use AI as a research tool. I do this before medical appointments. I arrive better informed, and my doctor and I can have a more useful conversation. However, I am not naive enough to act on what AI tells me without first consulting a medical professional.

  • If you are about to make a large or hard-to-reverse decision, such as rolling over a 401(k) or deciding how much you can safely spend in retirement, have a professional look at your situation first. AI offers confident, specific answers that carry no accountability, and it can be right most of the time and still be wrong on a detail that is costly to miss.

  • If you already know what you should do and are not doing it, an AI answer is unlikely to help. Look for a planner or financial therapist who listens and asks questions first, and who asks permission before giving advice.

AI is an evolving tool, not a magic source of instant answers. I strongly recommend that you let AI help do the research. Then bring that research to a professional advisor who will help you find solutions and strategies that are the best fit for you.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

The Republican brand has gone from shiny to tarnished to toxic

2026-10-29, updated: 2026-11-11

The Republican brand has gone from shiny to tarnished, to full-blown toxic.

Republicans used to be fiscally conservative with taxpayer’s money. They used to shun government mandates/controls over us. Republicans used to be respectful. You know, disagreeing without being disagreeable. Not anymore.

The leader of the Republican Party, President Donald Trump is TOTALLY responsible for making the party toxic.

Personal attacks, insults, mocking, and bullying are now the norm coming from him and his people.

To the toxicity add ignoring Congress and an open disdain for the courts that amounts to lawlessness. Think about his words that alienate our allies. Think about his praise of dictators.

His negative behavior has infected all of us. Civility is disappearing. Frustration, friction, and anger are growing.

Republicans used to be interested in building bridges. Now they only want to build walls with razor wire at the top and bottom.

The Republican-controlled Senate and House of Representatives can’t find the courage to tell Trump to STOP. They either agree with everything or are gutless.

Unless he dies, is impeached, or resigns, we are stuck with Trump and his ilk for two more years. Even if he leaves it is obvious Vice President Vance will continue the toxic behavior.

What can we, the voters, do?

It’s simple, we must vote out those supporting the toxicity, at the national and state level. That includes his followers running in the legislature.

Neither of our South Dakota Senators have publicly stood up to Trump. One of them is on the November ballot. Our current Republican Governor supports Trump and, therefore, his toxicity. Our current Republican Attorney General, who wants to be our next member of Congress, had his picture taken with Trump. Both of them giving the “Thumbs Up,” gesture.

Are all Republican elected officials bad, nasty people?

No. But none of them have publicly criticized or renounced Trump’s toxicity.

The only logical conclusion is that they support it or are gutless.

We can’t let that continue.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired

via Market Place Morning Report

Inflation, gas prices make Trump tax cut savings go pffft

2026-10-28, updated: 2026-11-11

Yeah, that was "one big beautiful bill,” alright. What those people in the picture above are preening about as President Trump signs the bill is more like one big beautiful bunch of baloney.

Locally, Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds repeatedly crow about how tax cuts created by Donald Trump's “big, beautiful bill,” were supposed to be a cash windfall for working families. Mike Rounds seems particularly infatuated with the notion, as a line about it seems to show up in every one of his televised ads as he seeks re-election.

You can’t blame Rounds – indeed, you can’t blame the entire Republican Party – for bragging on a tax cut that did, indeed, save working families some money.

Trouble is, their crowing stops short of reality: The money saved on taxes has evaporated into an atmosphere of inflated consumer prices.

After computing tax savings and the effects of inflation on middle-income Americans, the Institute for Taxation and Economic Policy, in a just released report, concludes that “ middle-income Americans are losing an average of $1,670 in 2026 overall, accounting for changes in tax policy and increased inflation that has been boosted by tariffs, the Iran war, and the loss of immigrant workers.”

You don’t have to be an economic analyst to know how inflation has hit your family’s bottom line … or to figure out that the Trump administration and its string of ill-conceived policies have been the driving force for higher prices across the board.

As to the political value of Republican braggadocio about Trump’s tax cuts, is it doing any good as the election draws near?

As a stand-alone issue, maybe. Overall, though, I doubt it. Polls coming in as mid-terms draw near show the GOP is behind, practically across the board. More specifically, last week’s AP poll shows 84% of respondents say that the cost of living is one of their top concerns.

Cory Heidelberger notes in Dakota Free Press that even in deep red South Dakota a majority of poll respondents say that Trump has hurt the economy.

My hunch is that most people, after they hear Republicans crowing about the money saved by the tax cut, quickly remind themselves and each other that, yeah, it meant more money all right, but what about the cost of food and gas eating it all up?

Followed by a competing, practically reflexive rejoinder like that, the GOP’s boasting about the “big beautiful bill” is a net political liability. In the political card game, inflation trumps the tax cut.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via NPR Economic

The rise of class warfare … and why the moneyed class is winning

2026-10-27, updated: 2026-11-11

The definition of conservative has changed dramatically over the last two decades. For centuries conservatism simply meant resistance to change—a desire to keep things as they are.

This was especially true of those upper classes whose life was better than others. They wished to keep it that way. Progressives desired change in a way that helped the classes not benefitting from the existing system.

This is nothing new as there has always been a level of class warfare in every society.

There are two kinds of class war—economic and social. The struggle was relatively benign in the United States for centuries. Starting with the Emancipation Proclamation the social struggle became more pronounced. It was the southern wing of the Democratic Party that struggled to hold on to its privileges as the class who enjoyed a high social class status.

With the passage of the Civil Rights Act the southern white class lost much of its superior place in southern society. This strongly exacerbated the struggle with respect to race.

Because it was pushed by a Democratic president, LBJ, many southern whites switched to the Republican Party in the 1970s. Over the last half century that racial social war has not gone away, but has been vastly reduced in scope. Meanwhile, the economic struggle expanded. Under Theodore Roosevelt, the Republican Party became fairly progressive, initiating reforms designed to improve the lives of the working classes.

As the Twentieth Century moved forward, progressive initiatives started to shift to the Democratic Party with the New Deal and other progressive actions of Franklin Roosevelt. These lessened the economic class differential.

The struggle was still relatively benign until the 21st century. The emergence of the Tea Party wing of the Republican Party in 2010 saw an escalation in the economic classs struggle. Those who enjoyed a comfortable lifestyle resented their tax dollars being spent on those they deemed less deserving. Over the last two decades this feeling has grown into serious economic class warfare, with Democrats seeking to make the economic classes less separated and Republicans seeking to preserve the status quo and keep their money to themselves.

Over the preceding decades, progressive successes achieved by liberals — Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps and a variety of other programs — helped the lower economic classes enjoy a higher standard of living. However, this was at the expense of the higher income classes who were understandably opposed. There have been constant conservative efforts to reduce Medicaid and food stamps, now called SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) as well as school lunch and other programs.

In South Dakota the struggle has been shown in many actions. Recent examples are:

Sales tax on food. The legislature has had numerous bills to eliminate the sales tax on food. It has always been rejected because it would seriously reduce state revenues and might require a new source of revenue. An income tax has always been verboten. However, increased revenue from internet sales provided an opportunity to eliminate the sales tax on groceries. Even the Republican governor endorsed the idea. It would reduce costs an average of about $300 per year for a family of four. However this would be relatively equal among all economic classes, disproportionately benefiting the poor. The upper economic classes would not benefit proportionately; it was essentially progressive. This was unacceptable to the legislature and the legislature changed the bill to reduce the overall tax rate by 0.3%. This has the effect of giving more tax reduction to those who spend large amounts of money—businesses and high-income people. A person buying a $100,000 car, boat or machine would save $300 on one item alone. The high income classes won the war over the use of the increased internet sales revenue. The lower economic classes lost in this economic war.

Expanding Medicaid. In 2009 The Medicaid program was expanded to allow states to participate with 90% federal funds to expand Medicaid to the working poor who earned too much to qualify for Medicaid but did not have employer provided health insurance. This would have helped tens of thousands of South Dakotans struggling with day to day living. In economic terms only, the Republican legislature should have endorsed a 9:1 ratio—getting nine dollars for every dollar spent. But this money virtually all went to help the lowest income people in the state. The legislature defeated that bill every year. The money would be better spent on “economic development,” meaning making the wealthy even richer. Finally, the people adopted a constitutional amendment requiring the state to participate. The lower income classes won. However, the legislature did not accept this decision by the people. When the administration proposed reductions to federal funding of the program the legislature proposed its own constitutional amendment (Amendment I on the ballot) ending funding if federal funding is ever reduced. Since funding reduction is a certainty by this administration, passing Amendment I would effectively repeal the citizen-passed amendment. If Amendment I passes, the lower income classes will lose again.

Property tax relief. In 2026 the governor proposed a series of property tax relief measures designed to reduce the property tax on owner occupied residences. They all shift property taxes to sales taxes. All of these programs would give the largest tax relief to the highest income classes of people—distinctly regressive. The lower classes lose. Worse yet, the poorest people in the state rent. When the taxes on their apartment increase, their rent increases. They pay higher taxes and also pay the sales tax and get NO benefit. The poorest people in the state are paying increased sales taxes to pay the property taxes of the richest people in the state.

Pure economic class warfare sponsored by our legislature. From a purely practical standpoint, this makes perfect financial sense. Legislators are elected. And in the vast majority of cases, the candidate with the most money in their campaign chest wins the election and candidates must raise large amounts of money. This comes from people with large amounts of money, and their wishes then dominate the discussion of policy issues. Poor people don’t contribute to political campaigns. They can’t buy influence. If I’m a legislator and need to choose whether to support a large campaign contributor or support the poor, screw the poor.

It is also true at the national level. Congress funds trillions of dollars on wars. Those wars produce millions of veterans. While large portion of their war expenditures come back to them from military contractors, virtually none comes back from veterans. As a result, while trillions are spent on wars creating millions of additional veterans, there have been relatively small increases to the VA in support for veterans. Our Defense Department now spends a trillion dollars; the VA a third of that. (the Defense Department has been correctly renamed the War Department since our military hasn’t defended us from a foreign military invasion since 1812. There is a reason we are called veterans of FOREIGN wars!!)

The class conflict between supporting people at the lower end of the economic ladder and supporting money at the upper end seems to have become more exaggerated in recent decades, but has no obvious solution. Both federally and locally, the money class is winning the struggle. Like all political issues the pendulum seems to swing back and forth. For decades, national policy tended to swing toward helping the less fortunate. Nationally it seems to be swinging back. Locally, the chances of swinging back in the foreseeable future seem remote.

John Cunningham of Sioux Falls has spent his career in local government finance, including in Fulton County, Ga., and Atlanta. He has a master of public administration from Harvard and has done consultant work in four foreign countries.

﻿Memo to Jackley and Rounds voters: You’re actually voting for Trump

2026-10-26, updated: 2026-11-11

South Dakotans can often interact directly with our Senators and Representatives.  Most of us have had personal proximity to them and many actually get to converse.

That understood, these two Republican candidates are regarded by most as regular guys, friendly and polite. By all accounts, and from my own personal experience, Mike Rounds and Marty Jackley are not aloof or hard to deal with and really give not much reason to be disliked. Rounds was regarded as a good governor, and Jackley should have had the opportunity, too.  So, South Dakota Republicans have found it mostly easy to vote for them.

However, this year, votes for Rounds and Jackley are not really votes for Rounds and Jackley.

A vote for either man is a vote for Donald Trump.

Trump’s presidency is, in the words of conservative columnist George Will a “cascading absurdity”. His bumbling, profane, “rallies” are a string of blatant lies and insults; every time he speaks in public it is another disgrace. He’s lied so much that newscasts don’t even bother to point it out. If he’s talking, it’s assumed he is lying, even by supporters who make excuses.

No need to list here all the damage Trump has done and continues to do to our democracy, our present, and our futures. It’s self evident more every day as his approval rating dives to historically low levels.

He’s been able to do this as a consequence of the utter corruption and degradation of the Republican Party. The ability to prevail despite all the mistakes and dangerous ignorance depends on the institutional support of the Republican establishment and its donors.

Neither Jackley nor Rounds (who has claimed that he votes with Trump “99% of the time”) has shown they would be anything other than two more silent partners and two more reliable votes for whatever Trump wants to do.  Some weak disagreement, maybe, but do we think either one will really strongly push back?

Come to attention, Republicans!  Your vote is an unavoidable package deal.

If you vote for these two candidates you are voting for:

  • Betraying Ukrainian patriots, in bed with Vladimir Putin.

  • Ruining our relationship with allies around the world, including our next door neighbors Canada and Mexico.

  • Continuing tariffs, raising prices for consumers, lowering prices for soybeans.

  • Pardoning friends and contributors and those who attacked the Capitol.

  • Family business enrichment , leading to a majority of the public’s perceptions of illegal or unethical behavior.

  • Multi trillion dollar deficits.

  • Historically mistaken war on Iran.

As you vote for Rounds and Jackley, you are implicitly voting for a continuation of all that. Nice guys, yes, but your vote really has not much to do with them. Trump is the Republican Party. Anything that enhances the strength of the party enables the actions of Trump.

It’s understandably difficult for a Republican to vote against either of the two candidates. You like them as individuals.  But do you have the integrity and courage to vote against Trump now knowing that neither of them will do so when the nation needs them?

Thank you for paying attention to this matter.

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

via Sacramento Bee

Major meeting in Sioux Falls Tuesday on proposed hyperscale data center

2026-10-24, updated: 2026-11-11

Editor’s note: You can observe the proceedings of the meeting and have an opportunity to speak. It’s set to discuss a proposed data center between Brandon and Sioux Falls on Tuesday, October 27, 7pm, Carnegie Town Hall, 235 W. 10th St. in Sioux Falls.

The issue of data centers has become a hot button, with the right and the left finding common ground. Democrats, Republicans, Independents and all others have coalesced around opposition to having them anywhere near our own communities.

And for good reasons: they suck the local energy sector dry, which will cause our electricity to fluctuate and cost us dearly in our pocketbooks … they do the same with the local water supply, and it’s unclear how much damage to water tables and our private supplies they will cause … they create noise at decibels well above the safety level for human well-being, and that also includes all the nearby wildlife and insects as well … and the profligate amount of diesel fuel they will house threatens our air and the environment with constant and unabated spills and leaks into the Earth.

On October 27, the Sioux Falls Council and the Lincoln County Commissioners will meet jointly to address the issue of data centers, particularly the Gemini Data Center, which is a proposed hyperscale data center on 164 acres between Brandon and Sioux Falls. There were hours of opposition remarks and testimony given to the SF Council this past January, yet the immediate vote in favor of the 500 megawatt Gemini project was 7-0.

Yet now the politicians have realized this has turned into a real issue with huge public opposition, so they’ve established an Oversight Committee to study potential future regulations on data centers and to gather more public input. This is what the October 27 meeting is all about and I suggest you, dear reader, make every effort to be there.

At least one of the public needs to suggest to the politicians that mitigation is the answer for all of us.

  1. on the power issue, any data center should have its own wind turbine (or more) and a solar roof and solar farm. These will not suffice on their own but will help mitigate the huge power needs of each data center.

  2. on the water issue, a closed loop system should always be employed and all the water used is to be recycled, so as little as possible is taken from the local supply.

  3. on the sound pollution issue, a 30-foot fence should be built around the entire data center itself. Such fences have proven to substantially mitigate the sound from interstate highways, so this fence (to include a closed gate) would help mitigate the noise.

  4. hundreds of diesel generators are expected for power augmentation purposes. Emission control devices can mitigate the air pollution of these generators, and fuel containment should be treated as part of critical infrastructure planning (for any and all future leaks).

There are many more issues concerning data centers, but these four stand out as the biggest and most critical. These politicians live here, too, and if they do not require these things, do you really think any company would voluntarily pay these expenses? Besides insisting that our local politicians pass regulations such as mentioned here, they should also eschew any thoughts of tax breaks.

The companies behind these centers represent billions of dollars and they fully intend to make a financial killing on these centers.

We cannot stop them, but we can regulate them and force them to mitigate the coming harm to our communities.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

via Electrek Feed

Media concentration. It's happening nationally and locally

2026-10-23, updated: 2026-11-11

The assertion that a strong democracy needs strong newspapers has been a popular cliche for generations. We might want to take the cliche seriously at a time when both our democracy and our independent news media appear to be in jeopardy.

Increasingly, independent newspapers are going out of business or being purchased by oligarchs and TV networks are consolidating into fewer and fewer hands. About 40% of America's newspapers have shut down since the year 2000. With support from the Trump administration, Paramount Skydance purchased Warner Brothers, including CNN, creating an enormous media empire. David Ellison of Skydance installed Bari Weiss, a right-wing influencer, at CBS News, where she has sought to control the content of news stories while many veteran journalists have resigned. Recently, Weiss has insisted that CBS News pursue negative stories on two Democratic U.S. Senate candidates who are running in highly competitive races: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. The recent allegation that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio proved to be utterly false.

Jeff Bezos, the founder and Chair of Amazon, now owns the Washington Post, which has been one of America's most esteemed newspapers for more than a century. Interestingly, the Post cost Bezos less than half of what he paid for his new super yacht. Bezos has steered the newspaper away from its perceived liberal bias, not wanting to irritate President Trump.

Across the country, investigative journalism is in trouble, and media organizations concentrate their energies, and their dwindling field reporters, on "feel good" human interest stories. When late night TV personalities like Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert chose to interview Talarico, those interviews were not allowed to air on their programs. Interestingly enough, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) abandoned the Fairness Doctrine, which required equal time for both sides of a political controversy, back in 1987. That does not affect the desire of media titans to avoid rocking the boat by giving exposure to politicians they do not like.

Here in South Dakota, the decline of independent media is obvious. Weekly newspapers in rural communities continue to shut their doors. Lee Enterprises, which owns the Rapid City Journal, had been saddled with debt ever since it purchased the Pulitzer newspaper chain at a time when readership was about to decline sharply. The Journal now comes out just three times a week, and it no longer covers state and local government as diligently as it did in the past. The staff of reporters is stretched mighty thin.

The masthead of the Rapid City Journal now includes a daily reminder that David Hoffmann of the Hoffmann Media Group is now the "majority shareholder" of the corporation. Interestingly, Lee Enterprises recently purchased the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, the Watertown Public Opinion and the Aberdeen American News, giving it a virtual monopoly of major papers in South Dakota similar to the monopoly that it enjoys in Montana. In South Dakota and nationally, there is a diminished news media in fewer hands. Fewer and fewer reporters are watching, and reporting on, our public policy makers. We can continue to hope that our democracy survives.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

via Market Place Tech Report

Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make

2026-10-22, updated: 2026-11-11

Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make. Are they going to stick with their now weak party labels or are they going to break ranks?

The U.S. Senate race includes the incumbent, Senator Mike Rounds. His votes have supported the numerous cutbacks in funding which have negatively affected all of us in one way or another. His silence on numerous important issues is beyond concerning. He wants another term.

The Democrats had a candidate who decided to step aside. Lots of reasons and some back stories to that decision.

Then there is the independent Brian Bengs. He has a solid military career. Was a JAG lawyer. He has been a college professor. He is assertive without being obnoxious. He is listening to us. He wants to take what he is hearing and be OUR voice in the Senate.

Here is the math: Democrats have about 130,000 members. Republicans have a little over 300,000. Independents and no party affiliation voters are about 150,000. 20,000 more than Democrats, and about half as many as Republicans.

Most people I listen to want change in Washington. They are tired of the daily/hourly drama. Their ability to pay bills is harder now because of continuing inflation. They are not happy about tariffs and cuts in programs which help us.

If we truly want change in Washington, Democrats will have to vote in large numbers for Bengs. Same for Independents. An important component is Republicans, many of whom are not happy with Rounds, will have to cross the forbidden line.

Pols done by reputable firms show Bengs either slightly ahead or within the “margin of error.”   It is possible an Independent can win this year.

In Nebraska and Idaho, the Independents running for U.S. Senate are both within the “margin of error.”

If Bengs and the other two can win, there will be five Independents in the U.S. Senate. Enough numbers that both parties will have to pay attention to them.

Voting really matters now. More than ever. Remember in the race for Mayor of Sioux Falls this summer, only FOUR votes separated the top two candidates.

I am optimistic that positive change is coming to Washington. It would be wonderful if South Dakota, you and I are part it.

So, to my diehard Democrat friends, hold your nose if you must and vote for change. To my Republican friends, we are in this mess because of leaders in what used to be a proud, honest, compassionate party. You may need to hold your nose too, and vote for change.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired

via Sacramento Bee

‘Anti-socialist’ Trump announces an $8 billion bailout for farmers.

2026-10-21, updated: 2026-11-11

Scrambling for votes at a Kansas Republican pep party last night, President Trump pledged that USDA will be making $8 billion in direct cash payments to American farmers. Combined with the $40 billion he’s already shelled out over the course of his two terms, Trump has given $48 billion in cash to farmers.

Much as I support cash assistance to American farmers – a stable ag economy is probably the  cornerstone of food and national security – this business of Trump financially harming our country’s ag sector with his counter-productive tariffs and inflation-driving foreign policies is getting old and expensive.

As to yesterday’s announcement, farmers shouldn’t be overly enthused about it. Scott Lincicome, VP of General Economics at the Cato Institute calls it “a band-aid on a flesh wound,” adding that at four thousand dollars a farm, “it might cover a few weeks of diesel costs.” As with other announcements (specifically, Russian diesel and imported ground beef) in recent months, Trump is fond of throwing out headline numbers that sound impressive but in actuality don’t do much in the way of helping farmers out with their double economic whammy of low crop prices and high input costs.

More generally, Trump’s reflexive need to look like he’s doing something substantive for producers and consumers has the unexpected political consequence of defining him as that word that he abhors — a socialist.

Disagree? If you consider socialism to be a system where the government intervenes in free market processes by altering free market outcomes, then Trump’s bailout is de facto socialism.

He has said “our country will never be a socialist country,” but, as with many of his other utterances, the president’s rhetoric often contradicts the president's reality.

Paying off farmers for financial troubles created by Trump’s flawed policies has been a recurring theme through both of his terms. He may hate the term, but when he needs to be, Trump is a socialist.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.
